title: Prevalence and perception among saudi arabian population about resharing of information on social media regarding natural remedies as protective measures against covid-19
screen_reason: Cross-sectional online survey of 1,249 adults in Saudi Arabia (275 health care workers, 974 non-health care workers), 25 March to 8 May 2020. One item asks respondents how often they have recirculated information about natural remedies as protective measures against COVID-19, and the paper reports that 59.7% of participants shared such information (40.3% never). The authors frame that content as rumour and unverified claim, so this is a self-reported SHARING measure, i.e. a RECALL row with recall_subtype sharing. It is flagged borderline: the survey item is defined by TOPIC, not by veracity, and the abstract itself says the study covers medical information 'whether true or false', so a respondent who shared an accurate post about herbal remedies is counted. The perception items are attitudes and reasons for sharing, not exposure, and are not extracted.

estimates.platform: Online survey about sharing on social media (WhatsApp 51.6%, Twitter 27.6%, Snapchat 13.8% named as the platforms used)
estimates.measure_type: % of survey respondents who report ever recirculating information about natural remedies as protective measures against COVID-19
estimates.value_raw: 59.7% of participants shared information on social media, with 22.5% doing it at all times, 8.2% usually, 5.7% often, 23.3% sometimes; 40.3% (503/1,249) never
estimates.denominator: 1,249 Saudi Arabian survey respondents aged 18+ (275 health care workers, 974 non-health care workers) recruited online
estimates.definition: Answered anything other than 'Never' (i.e. Sometimes, Often, Usually or Always) to 'Have you participated in recirculating the information related to natural remedies uses as protective measures during COVID-19 pandemic with others'
estimates.misinfo_def: herbal remedies was one of the rumors which was highly recirculated on social media and on different platforms; while herbal remedies and herbal products are not discouraged to be taken, they should not be considered a sole cure for COVID-19
estimates.source_quote: The study results showed that 59.7% of participants
estimates.page_loc: Discussion, p. 5132; underlying distribution in Table 2 'Prevalence of Circulating the Information...', p. 5131
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-report on a 10-item investigator-developed questionnaire (A. Alotiby), reviewed by three assistant professors, translated into Arabic and pretested with four Arabic-speaking experts and ten lay volunteers; Cronbach's alpha between 0.68 and 0.82 across items. No verification of what respondents actually shared.
estimates.moderator_quote: The study was made available to the general population, and HCWs of Saudi Arabia.
estimates.notes: Borderline on construct validity, not on arithmetic. The item asks about a TOPIC (natural remedies as protective measures against COVID-19), not about falsity; the abstract describes the object of study as medical information 'whether true or false'. The authors nevertheless treat the claim class as unverified and the paper's own comparison is with a 'worldwide prevalence' of misinformation sharing of 87.0%. Self-selected online sample (Google Survey link posted on social media plus an email to all HCWs registered with the Saudi Commission for Health Specialties), so no response rate can be computed and 77% of respondents are women. The 59.7% figure is stated verbatim in the Discussion; it is also the complement of the 40.3% 'Never' cell, but it was not computed by me. The survey text is imprecise about the window: no recall period is specified in the item.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (a) the HCW/NHCW split of the same item (61.9% of NHCWs vs 52.0% of HCWs recirculated; p = 0.049) - the paper's main contrast, but the pooled 59.7% is the headline prevalence and the subgroup sentence is broken across the two PDF columns, so I kept the total row only; (b) the individual frequency cells (Always 22.5%, Usually 8.2%, Often 5.7%, Sometimes 23.3%) - components of the same estimate, not separate estimates; (c) all of Table 4 (perception: 23.6% do not share until sure it is correct; 10.2% think sharing without evidence is harmless and may be beneficial; 6.7% think most published medical information is correct) - these are attitudes and reasons, neither exposure nor a perceived amount of misinformation in the environment, so under the instructions they do not license a RECALL row; (d) Table 5 demographic breakdowns of the sharing item (by region, gender, age 54.6-79.4%, education, HCW specialty) - demographic subgroups, not the headline; (e) Table 3 platform preferences (WhatsApp 51.6% etc.) - which platform was used, not a misinformation share; (f) the 87.0% 'worldwide prevalence' the authors compare against - a figure cited from another paper, excluded by rule. Problems a human should see: the methods contradict themselves on instrument length ('A 10-item questionnaire' in one paragraph, 'The nine questions were divided into two sections' in the next); the reliability report is left with unfilled placeholders ('a minimum reliability score of 0.68 for (nominate a question)'); Table 4's note says values are significant at P = 0.010 while the text says 'All the values in Table 4 are statistically significant at P = 0.10'; the Introduction dates the pandemic to December 2020 though data were collected in March-May 2020; and the sentence 'approximately of the study participants recirculated the information' is missing its number.

rob.design: Descriptive cross-sectional online survey, 25 March - 8 May 2020, Saudi Arabia. Convenience/self-selected recruitment: a Google Survey URL posted on social media plus an email from the Saudi Commission for Health Specialties to all registered health care workers; online informed consent; under-18s excluded. N = 1,249 after data revision (275 HCWs, 974 NHCWs); 95.4% Saudi nationals, 76.9% female, 66% aged 18-40. A power calculation targeted 385 per group. Instrument: investigator-developed questionnaire (described as 10-item in one place and nine questions in another), expert-reviewed, translated to Arabic and pretested, Cronbach's alpha 0.68-0.82. Analysis: descriptive frequencies and Pearson chi-square. No response rate is reportable, and exposure/sharing is entirely self-reported with no veracity check.
